forces: Tenor soloist, mixed chorus and orchestra
performers: Michel Sénéchal, tenor; Chorale Élisabeth Brasseur; Orchestre des Concerts Lamoureux; Igor Markevitch, conductor
question: How does the same prayer expand from low voices to the full ensemble?
intro: A prayer for the whole universe moves from low choral declamation through a flute interlude and a tenor solo towards a large communal close. Boulanger’s score alternates words and wordless humming; listen for how those different kinds of vocal sound join the sections.

cues.title: A low collective voice
cues.text: The prayer begins with altos and basses together, over a restrained orchestral foundation. Repeated notes and a compact melodic shape matter more than a long lyrical tune. Listen for how repetition makes the line feel like sustained address.
cues.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed p. 1; the opening has a C-centred Phrygian inflection: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/44/IMSLP21037-PMLP48704-Boulanger_Vielle_Pri%C3%A8re_Bouddhique.pdf. Whole-work listening point, not an assertion that a particular note or entrance occurs at this timestamp.

cues.title: A French Buddhist text
cues.text: Suzanne Karpelès supplied the French text used by Boulanger. The score calls the work a daily prayer for the whole universe. Its setting belongs to a French concert tradition; the orchestral colours are not evidence of a documented Buddhist performance practice.
cues.evidence: Konstantin Galluhn preface; translator credit on score p. 1: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/44/IMSLP21037-PMLP48704-Boulanger_Vielle_Pri%C3%A8re_Bouddhique.pdf https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/987.html

cues.title: Humming joins the phrases
cues.text: Wordless humming is part of the score’s design, not background noise. Sopranos and tenors enter with closed mouths while the lower voices carry the words. Across the work, that sustained vocal colour helps one span pass into another.
cues.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, opening, bar 9, and printed p. 17; structural account: https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/987.html: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/44/IMSLP21037-PMLP48704-Boulanger_Vielle_Pri%C3%A8re_Bouddhique.pdf. Whole-work listening point, not an assertion that a particular note or entrance occurs at this timestamp.

cues.title: A broader first span
cues.text: The opening prayer has expanded into a stronger, brighter stretch. Follow the growth across the phrase instead of hearing every change of volume as a new section.
cues.evidence: Actual cached mono stream: cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-vieille-priere.txt, a marked change at 1:26 leads into stronger 1:30–2:10 windows, reaching −4.6 dB near 2:10 Source file: https://archive.org/details/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d. These measurements establish the broad contour, not isolated instruments or words.

cues.title: The flute continues the thread
cues.text: The instrumental interlude takes up the earlier melodic material in a freely shaped flute line. Harp motion and divided strings keep an accompaniment beneath it. Listen for a change of speaker rather than a break in the prayer’s continuity.
cues.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 8–10, flute solo after the second choral stanza: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/44/IMSLP21037-PMLP48704-Boulanger_Vielle_Pri%C3%A8re_Bouddhique.pdf. cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-vieille-priere.txt: the withdrawal around 2:25 and boundary at 2:28 locate the interlude approximately. Approximate passage placement; no bar-to-audio alignment or exact entrance is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rome to Arcachon
cues.text: Begun in Rome in 1914, the work was completed in Arcachon in 1917. Those places and dates are written at the end of the score. Its long gestation crossed the war years; the music should not be reduced to a diary entry.

cues.title: A single tenor speaks
cues.text: The tenor’s central span shifts the prayer from collective declamation to one voice. Michel Sénéchal sings this recording’s solo; the score surrounds the line with divided strings and restrained wind colours rather than the opening’s choral mass.
cues.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 11–12, figure 4, A Tempo: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/44/IMSLP21037-PMLP48704-Boulanger_Vielle_Pri%C3%A8re_Bouddhique.pdf. cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-vieille-priere.txt: the strong changes around 3:14–3:18 and quiet subsequent windows support the approximate start of the solo region. Approximate passage placement; no bar-to-audio alignment or exact entrance is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A deep withdrawal
cues.text: This central passage makes room for very soft sound. Keep following the line through the withdrawal: low recorded level does not itself mean a pause or the end of a stanza.
cues.evidence: Actual cached mono stream: cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-vieille-priere.txt, relative level falls to about −16.9 dB at 4:10 before recovering; the analysis does not identify a particular sung word Source file: https://archive.org/details/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d. These measurements establish the broad contour, not isolated instruments or words.

cues.title: First heard after her death
cues.text: Boulanger never heard the completed work in concert. The scholarly preface records the first performance on 9 June 1921, conducted by Henri Büsser with the Concerts Dandelot orchestra, more than three years after her death.
cues.evidence: Performance history in Konstantin Galluhn’s preface. https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/987.html

cues.title: From humming to full speech
cues.text: Near the later return, humming and a held pause make room for a much fuller choral statement. The complete choir and strings take up the line together. Compare this unified weight with the low voices and more restrained accompaniment at the beginning.
cues.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 17–18, figure 7 and following choral entry: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/44/IMSLP21037-PMLP48704-Boulanger_Vielle_Pri%C3%A8re_Bouddhique.pdf. cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-vieille-priere.txt: the quiet 5:25 window is followed by the large 5:30 level and brightness jump; no exact first-word timing is claimed. Approximate passage placement; no bar-to-audio alignment or exact entrance is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The larger voice persists
cues.text: The expanded sound holds its force through this later stretch. Listen for the difference between a sustained communal statement and a single loud accent: the preceding quiet span has changed the scale of what follows.
cues.evidence: Actual cached mono stream: cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-vieille-priere.txt, the 5:35–6:10 windows sustain substantially higher levels than the preceding central passage Source file: https://archive.org/details/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d. These measurements establish the broad contour, not isolated instruments or words.

cues.title: A coda without words
cues.text: The final coda abandons words for open vowels and increases its motion. Acceleration, repeated attacks and crescendo lead to a broad final chord. This score ends with a forceful affirmation, not a long pianissimo fade.
cues.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 23–24, Accel., figure 10 and Large: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/44/IMSLP21037-PMLP48704-Boulanger_Vielle_Pri%C3%A8re_Bouddhique.pdf. cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-vieille-priere.txt: onset activity increases around 6:50–7:00, while the last strong windows precede the final recorded decay around 7:10. Approximate passage placement; no bar-to-audio alignment or exact entrance is claimed.

transitions.title: The flute inherits the sung line
transitions.how: The second choral span tapers into sustained humming. A solo flute then varies the preceding melodic figures above harp motion, divided strings and quieter wind support. The choir does not need a full stop to hand over the foreground: the held vocal sound and continuing accompaniment turn the instrumental passage into a link.
transitions.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 8–10: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/44/IMSLP21037-PMLP48704-Boulanger_Vielle_Pri%C3%A8re_Bouddhique.pdf. Actual cached analysis, cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-vieille-priere.txt: the level drops after 2:10 and the 2:28 change locates the interlude approximately. The written mechanism is documented; its placement in this recording is approximate, not a timed word or bar alignment.

transitions.title: The flute’s freedom becomes a vocal line
transitions.how: After the flute’s increasingly mobile figure, a yielding gesture leads to A Tempo at figure 4. The tenor begins a calm, clear line while divided strings alternate bowed and plucked sounds beneath it. Winds retain sustained notes and answering phrases. A change of foreground and accompaniment, not a hard silence, introduces the solo prayer.
transitions.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 10–12, figure 4: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/44/IMSLP21037-PMLP48704-Boulanger_Vielle_Pri%C3%A8re_Bouddhique.pdf. Actual cached analysis, cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-vieille-priere.txt: strong novelty around 3:14–3:18 and a quieter following stretch provide the approximate anchor. The written mechanism is documented; its placement in this recording is approximate, not a timed word or bar alignment.

transitions.title: A held breath releases the full choir
transitions.how: The solo region gives way to overlapping voices and closed-mouth humming. After a long held pause, the full choir and strings state the line together, marked loudly and declaimed. Brass and percussion reinforce the larger sound. Boulanger makes the contrast through a held breath, unified vocal rhythm and expanded scoring.
transitions.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 17–18, held pause and full-choir statement: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/44/IMSLP21037-PMLP48704-Boulanger_Vielle_Pri%C3%A8re_Bouddhique.pdf. Actual cached analysis, cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-vieille-priere.txt: the 5:25 window is quiet; at 5:30 level rises to −3.9 dB and brightness to about 1769 Hz. The written mechanism is documented; its placement in this recording is approximate, not a timed word or bar alignment.

transitions.title: Words release an accelerating final gesture
transitions.how: The last textual statement leads into open-vowel choral sound. Repeated orchestral attacks gather speed under an acceleration, with a crescendo through the brass, winds and strings. The final Large broadens the arrival into a forceful chord. The change from words to sustained vowels allows the orchestra’s rhythmic energy to finish the argument.
transitions.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 23–24, Accel. through Large: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/44/IMSLP21037-PMLP48704-Boulanger_Vielle_Pri%C3%A8re_Bouddhique.pdf. Actual cached analysis, cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-vieille-priere.txt: higher onset activity around 6:50–7:00 and strong late windows locate the closing drive approximately. The written mechanism is documented; its placement in this recording is approximate, not a timed word or bar alignment.

timeline.note: Altos and basses begin together above the held orchestral foundation; no instrumental prelude.
Upper choral humming complements the lower voices; this is a broad opening snapshot, not an exact bar-9 entrance.
The central flute interlude unfolds over two harps and divided strings; choral sound tapers at its beginning.
The tenor’s calm central statement replaces the flute foreground; divided strings retain bowed and plucked layers.
Towards the end of the solo region, choral imitation and humming prepare the communal return.
After the held pause, full choir and strings declaim together with lower brass and percussion reinforcement.
The accelerating wordless coda gathers the full ensemble, then broadens for the final chord.

composer.epithet: Her songs and psalms give a sustained bass, a repeated interval and the weight of a choral unison the force of a large formal argument.
facts: Daughter of Ernest and Raïssa Boulanger; younger sister of the composer, conductor and teacher Nadia Boulanger
Paris Conservatoire; composition with Paul Vidal, with extensive musical support from Nadia
First woman to win the Premier Grand Prix de Rome for musical composition, 1913
Songs, choral works, orchestral and chamber pieces; unfinished opera La Princesse Maleine
composer.background:
Lili Boulanger grew up in a Paris household where composition, singing and teaching were family work. Her father Ernest had won the Prix de Rome in 1835 and taught singing at the Conservatoire; her mother Raïssa had been his pupil. Nadia, born in 1887, was already receiving serious musical training when Lili was small. Lili learned piano and several other instruments and accompanied her sister into Conservatoire classes. Recurrent illness interrupted her education from childhood. The resulting timetable was irregular, but the musical environment was exceptionally well supplied with teachers, performers and scores.

Nadia was an early mentor and practical support; Lili’s formal composition teacher at the Conservatoire was Paul Vidal. Their training included fugue, harmony and the cantata, extending well beyond the short piano pieces through which women composers were often permitted a public identity. In 1912 illness forced Lili to withdraw from the final stage of the Prix de Rome. She returned in 1913 and won the Premier Grand Prix with Faust et Hélène, becoming the first woman to receive that composition prize. She was nineteen. Nadia had won a second prize in 1908.
